claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness.
Dislocations accumulate or pile up near internal lamellar boundaries during straining.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations.
Local stress concentrations promote microcrack initiation and catastrophic damage.
Post-deformation low-temperature annealing can modify the lamellar-colony microstructure.
Post-deformation low-temperature annealing can form gradient interface structures along the internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies.
Annealing rearranges or relaxes the internal boundary structure.
The annealing-induced interface structure reduces barriers responsible for dislocation pile-ups.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups decreases local stress concentrations.
Lower local stress concentrations delay microcrack initiation and catastrophic failure.
The annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile elongation than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or marginally increase strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Annealing temperature and time can be selected to alter the interface structure while preserving phase stability.
The treatment is expected to be effective under room-temperature tensile loading.
Performance under different strain rates, cyclic loading, and elevated temperatures remains unverified.
The annealing temperature and time window needed to balance pile-up reduction against deleterious phase transformations is not known precisely.
